title: The Tuskegee syphilis study

confidence.note: The study's own publications, Public Health Service files now in the National Archives, the 1972 press reports and the congressional hearings document it thoroughly. Estimates of how many men died of syphilis vary, from at least 28 to perhaps 100 by 1969.

people: Peter Buxtun, Public Health Service interviewer who exposed the study
Eunice Rivers, nurse who worked alongside the study's doctors in Macon County
Susan Reverby, historian who uncovered the Guatemala experiments
summary: For forty years US government doctors watched hundreds of Black men live with syphilis, deceiving them and keeping them from penicillin, until a whistleblower went to the press.
body: In 1932 the US Public Health Service began following 600 Black men in Macon County, Alabama, a poor rural county still tied to its plantation past: 399 who already had syphilis and 201 without it as controls. With the cooperation of the Tuskegee Institute, government doctors told the men they had "bad blood," passed off diagnostic spinal taps as free treatment, and promised burial expenses to secure autopsies.

By 1944 penicillin was the therapy of choice for syphilis, yet there was no discussion of treating the men; local doctors were told "He's under study and not to be treated." By 1969 at least 28 and perhaps 100 had died of the disease. Peter Buxtun, a Public Health Service interviewer, protested internally from 1966 and finally went to a journalist. The story broke on 25 July 1972, and that October a federal panel advised ending the study.

Senate hearings led to the National Research Act of 1974, institutional review boards and the Belmont Report of 1979. President Clinton apologized in 1997. In 2010 the historian Susan Reverby revealed that Public Health Service researchers had deliberately infected hundreds of Guatemalans with syphilis and gonorrhea in 1946–48.

myth.tradition: Government doctors injected the Alabama men with syphilis.
myth.record: The 399 men in the syphilis group already had the disease when they were enrolled; the wrong done to them was deception and the withholding of treatment. Deliberate infection did happen, in the Public Health Service's experiments in Guatemala in 1946–48.

links.note: The cure that existed from the 1940s and was kept from the men.
The 1947 code on consent; there is no evidence the study was ever discussed in its light.
Another case often cited in Black Americans' distrust of medicine.

title: Sulfa drugs

confidence.note: Domagk's laboratory work, his 1935 paper, the Pasteur Institute's 1935 report and the FDA's investigation of the 1937 poisonings are all contemporary. The story of his daughter's cure comes from later biographical accounts such as the Nobel Foundation's; he left it out of his own report.

place: Wuppertal, Germany; Paris; Bristol, Tennessee, USA
people: Gerhard Domagk (1895–1964), IG Farben pathologist who found Prontosil's effect
Jacques Tréfouël, Federico Nitti and Daniel Bovet, Pasteur Institute researchers who reported sulfanilamide's effect in 1935
Harold Cole Watkins, Massengill chemist who made Elixir Sulfanilamide
summary: A red dye cured streptococcal infections, a Paris lab found the simple molecule inside it, and a poisonous 'elixir' version pushed Congress to give the FDA new powers over drugs.
body: On 20 December 1932, at an IG Farben laboratory in Wuppertal, Gerhard Domagk found that a red dye, Prontosil, protected mice from lethal streptococcal infection. According to the Nobel Foundation's biography, when his own daughter, aged six, fell gravely ill with a streptococcal infection he gave her the drug and she recovered; he left that out of his report and published only in 1935, once clinicians had results. That year Bovet's group at the Pasteur Institute in Paris found that plain sulfanilamide, first made in 1908, worked as well as the dye. Sulfa drugs became a turning point against childbed fever, pneumonia, meningitis and gonorrhea. Domagk won the 1939 Nobel Prize, but German authorities made him decline it; he received it in 1947.

In 1937 the S.E. Massengill Company of Bristol, Tennessee, dissolved sulfanilamide in diethylene glycol, a chemical normally used as antifreeze and a deadly poison, and shipped "Elixir Sulfanilamide" without toxicity testing, which the law did not require. More than 100 people in 15 states died, many of them children treated for sore throats. The company's chemist killed himself. The scandal hastened the 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which increased the FDA's authority to regulate drugs.

title: Lobotomy

confidence.note: Moniz's 1936 reports, Freeman and Watts's publications and the 1949 Nobel citation document the history. The US total of 40,000–50,000 operations is a historians' estimate, not an exact count.

people: Egas Moniz (1874–1955), Portuguese neurologist
Almeida Lima, neurosurgeon who performed Moniz's operations
Walter Freeman, American neurologist and promoter of the transorbital lobotomy
James Watts, American neurosurgeon
summary: A Nobel-winning brain operation spread to tens of thousands of psychiatric patients, many cut through the eye socket outside any operating room, before drugs made it obsolete.
body: In November 1935 the Lisbon neurologist Egas Moniz, with the neurosurgeon Almeida Lima operating, began destroying white matter in the frontal lobes of psychiatric patients, at first by injecting alcohol. Earlier that year in London he had heard Jacobsen and Fulton describe chimpanzees that stopped reacting aggressively to their mistakes after frontal-lobe surgery, a report many have seen as the spur to his "bold step." In 1936 he reported improvement in 14 of his first 20 patients. Asylums were overcrowded and conventional treatments were few.

In the United States the neurologist Walter Freeman and neurosurgeon James Watts adopted and enlarged the operation. In 1946 Freeman turned to a transorbital method from the Italian psychiatrist Amarro Fiamberti, driving an ice-pick-like instrument through the eye socket; it needed no anesthetist, no surgeon and not even proper sterile technique, and Watts ended their partnership. An estimated 40,000–50,000 lobotomies were performed in the US between 1936 and 1959, 3,500–4,000 of them by Freeman.
Moniz shared the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Chlorpromazine, introduced in 1952, offered a drug alternative, and the operation dwindled to a rarity.

links.note: Overcrowded asylums made a quick operation attractive.
Another 1930s physical treatment for mental illness.
The drug that made lobotomy largely obsolete.

title: Electroconvulsive therapy

confidence.note: The first treatments in April 1938 were reported promptly and documented by the press at the time; the first stimulation on 11 April did not itself produce a seizure, so 'first treatment' and 'first seizure' differ by nine days. Evidence that ECT works for severe depression comes from randomized trials between the 1960s and 1980s.

people: Ugo Cerletti (1877–1963), Italian neuropsychiatrist
Lucio Bini, his assistant
summary: Two Rome psychiatrists swapped risky seizure-inducing drugs for an electric current, creating a treatment that was misused, caricatured in film and later shown to work.
body: Psychiatrists in the 1930s induced seizures with camphor or cardiazol, but chemical seizures were unpredictable and the wait for the fit stressful. At the university clinic in Rome, Ugo Cerletti and his assistant Lucio Bini, after animal studies that included watching pigs at the Testaccio slaughterhouse, first applied current to a psychotic patient on 11 April 1938; a full seizure came on 20 April, and he recovered after further treatments. Anesthesia and muscle relaxation followed by the early 1950s. Trials since the 1960s support ECT mainly for severe depression, though misuse and films like *One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest* darkened its image.

links.note: The other physical treatment of 1930s psychiatry.
Born in the age of asylums desperate for treatments.

title: The Pap smear

confidence.note: Papanicolaou's 1928 talk and his 1941 paper and 1943 monograph with Traut are on record. Babeș is said to have presented similar findings at the same time, so the test's single name hides a shared discovery. Screening programs are credited with a dramatic fall in cervical cancer mortality, but the size of the effect owes much to organized screening and not only to the test, and the sources give no figures.

people: George Papanicolaou (1883–1962), Greek-born anatomist at Cornell
Herbert Traut, gynecologic pathologist and collaborator
Aurel Babeș, Romanian pathologist
summary: In 1928 a Cornell scientist reported that cancer cells could be spotted in a simple smear; skeptics doubted him, but the test became a cornerstone of cervical cancer screening.
body: George Papanicolaou, a Greek-born researcher at Cornell, found while studying vaginal cells that cancer cells could be detected in a simple smear, and presented the technique in 1928 at a conference in Battle Creek, Michigan. Pathologists, who relied on tissue, doubted that shed cells could diagnose cancer, and he neglected the finding for several years. The Romanian pathologist Aurel Babeș presented similar findings at about the same time, sampling the cervix. With the pathologist Herbert Traut he published convincing results in 1941 and a monograph in 1943, and screening programs built on the test contributed to a steep fall in cervical cancer deaths.

links.note: Prevention moved from finding abnormal cells to stopping the virus behind them.

title: Chemotherapy from a war gas

confidence.note: The patient's hospital chart, rediscovered at Yale and written up in 2011, fixes the first dose to 27 August 1942. The work was secret and the results were published only between 1946 and 1948, and some scholarly accounts still link the birth of chemotherapy to the 1943 Bari disaster. Calling it the first chemotherapy depends on defining the term as a synthetic drug given against a cancer.

people: Alfred Gilman, Yale pharmacologist
Louis Goodman, Yale physician and pharmacologist
Gustaf Lindskog, Yale surgeon who treated the first patient
Thomas Dougherty, Yale anatomist who collaborated on the mouse experiments
Sidney Farber, Boston pathologist
summary: In secret wartime work at Yale, a chemical weapon's cousin became the earliest documented drug to shrink a human cancer, opening the era of chemotherapy.
body: Poison gas, mustard gas prominent among it, caused over a million casualties in the First World War, and in 1919 an army doctor reported that mustard gas wiped out white blood cells. During the Second, a US government research agency funded Yale pharmacologists Alfred Gilman and Louis Goodman to study its chemical cousin, nitrogen mustard. In rabbits it depleted white blood cells; in mice with transplanted lymphomas it shrank tumors. On 27 August 1942 the surgeon Gustaf Lindskog gave it to a patient known as JD, a Polish-born factory worker dying of lymphosarcoma. His tumors regressed, then came back; he died on 1 December 1942, his bone marrow wiped out.

The work was secret, and results were published only between 1946 and 1948. At Bari in December 1943 a ship carrying mustard bombs was hit and almost a thousand exposed people later died of bone-marrow failure. In 1948 Sidney Farber in Boston used aminopterin, a folate antagonist, against childhood leukemia, introducing the first antimetabolite. Early drugs usually gave only transient responses, but the principle was established: chemicals could attack cancer.

myth.tradition: Chemotherapy was born when doctors noticed what the 1943 Bari gas disaster did to survivors' blood.
myth.record: Yale's first treatment of a cancer patient with nitrogen mustard took place in August 1942, more than a year before the Bari raid.

links.note: An earlier chemical attack on disease, in the same hope of selective drugs.
Targeted drugs grew from the chemotherapy tradition.

title: Kolff's artificial kidney

confidence.note: Kolff's patient records, published and recently retold from his archive, date the first treatments to 1943 and the first survivor to September 1945. He built on earlier attempts, including a human dialysis by Georg Haas in 1924.

people: Willem Kolff (1911–2009), Dutch physician
Sofia Schafstadt, the first survivor
Belding Scribner, Seattle nephrologist
Wayne Quinton, Seattle engineer
summary: In occupied Holland a young doctor washed blood through sausage casing; sixteen patients died before the seventeenth woke from a uremic coma.
body: In the German-occupied Netherlands, Willem Kolff built a rotating-drum artificial kidney at the small hospital in Kampen, using cellophane sausage casing as the filter and scavenged parts, among them aluminum from a downed plane. He began treating patients in 1943; 16 died before the 17th, Sofia Schafstadt, came out of a uremic coma and recovered on 18 September 1945. Dialysis for permanent kidney failure began in Seattle in 1960, when Belding Scribner and Wayne Quinton devised a reusable shunt, and a lay committee chose who got the scarce treatment.

myth.record: John Abel's team dialyzed animals from 1913 and Georg Haas dialyzed a human in 1924. Kolff's team produced what Wieringa and colleagues call the first patient anywhere to survive uremic coma from acute kidney failure thanks to dialysis.

title: The blue baby operation

confidence.note: The operation was reported by Blalock and Taussig in JAMA about six months later and is well documented at Johns Hopkins; most accounts give 29 November 1944, though one recent article says 9 November. Thomas's central role is described in recent histories but went unacknowledged in the operation's name for decades.

people: Helen Taussig (1898–1986), pediatric cardiologist who proposed the operation
Alfred Blalock (1899–1964), surgeon
Vivien Thomas (born 1910), surgical technician who developed it in dogs
Eileen Saxon, the first patient
summary: A cardiologist's idea, a Black technician's laboratory work and a surgeon's hands produced the first effective treatment for cyanotic 'blue babies'.
body: Children born with tetralogy of Fallot turn blue because too little blood reaches their lungs. The cardiologist Helen Taussig proposed rerouting an artery to fix that, and at Johns Hopkins Vivien Thomas, a Black technician paid as a janitor, spent a year working out the operation on almost 200 dogs. On 29 November 1944 Alfred Blalock joined the subclavian artery of 15-month-old Eileen Saxon to her pulmonary artery, with Thomas beside him guiding the procedure. Her color improved, but after two months the cyanosis returned. Thomas's name was first proposed for the shunt only in 2003.

links.note: Palliation came first; open repair needed the heart-lung machine.
Catheter studies soon refined diagnosis of the same defects.
